description: Executor-level VelesQL conformance: asserts result ROWS / COUNTS / ORDERING, not just that a query parses. Golden ids are derived from velesdb-core (the source of truth); other executors (WASM, CLI) must reproduce the same result set for the same dataset+query. Shared read-only dataset; ordering is on unique payload fields so results are deterministic. `cases` must pass; `known_bugs` carry the expected result for a former core bug that is now FIXED — the regression-lock test (test_velesql_executor_known_bugs) runs un-ignored and must keep passing. Since v2.0.0 (issue #1544) the fixture also carries `extra_collections` + `join_cases` (JOIN ON/USING, core+WASM only — the CLI harness is intentionally untouched, see below), `aggregate_cases` (GROUP BY/HAVING via `execute_aggregate`, core+WASM only), `setops_cases` (UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT, core+WASM only, ids in order since D003 was resolved), `match_cases` (1-2 hop MATCH, core+WASM only, per-executor query text — see D004 for why), and `documented_divergences` (informational: known, accepted core/WASM behavioural gaps, not pass/fail cases). `cases`/`dataset`/`known_bugs` are byte-for-byte compatible with v1.0.0 so the existing CLI conformance suite (which only reads those three keys) keeps running unmodified against the original 10 cases plus the new scalar-expression cases X011-X014, which use the same single-collection `docs` dataset and are safe for CLI's strict-order comparison. v2.1.0 adds LIKE/ILIKE/OFFSET (X015-X020) and NEAR under OR, alone and inside an AND (X021-X022), to `cases`, so the CLI runs them too, and, core+WASM only, the statement families the WASM executor implements on its own: `query_params` (the vectors every case below may bind), `near_cases` (NEAR ranking, hybrid NEAR + metadata, similarity() thresholds; ids in order plus `expect_scores`, compared within 1e-5), `fusion_cases` (NEAR_FUSED rrf/average/maximum and a trailing USING FUSION), `rejected_cases` (queries both engines must refuse), `dml_cases` (UPDATE/DELETE `statements` run on a fresh copy of the dataset, then `query` is asserted) and `projection_cases` (DISTINCT and named-column projection, compared as projected JSON rows). Also core+WASM only: `vector_group_cases` run a vector GROUP BY (NEAR + GROUP BY) and compare the order of its groups by `group_column`, and every `rejected_cases` entry names the `expected_code` both engines must refuse it with. v2.7.0 adds R032 (V019, an aggregation as a compound operand). v2.6.0 adds the `nums` extra collection and `number_cases` (plain SELECT, core+WASM, ids in order): numbers compare by exact value, `-0.0` equal to `0`, `0.3` not `0.30000000000000004`, an integer past 2^53 not the float it rounds to, an IN list the same at any length; core also runs them through a secondary index and the payload mirror. It adds G022-G025 (GROUP BY, MIN/MAX and HAVING over those numbers) and P006-P007 (DISTINCT `id`, PARTITION BY a number), and runs `projection_cases` over the extra collections too. v2.5.0 adds the `tickets` extra collection, whose payloads carry an `id` of their own, with O003 and G021 (`id` is the point id in WHERE, ORDER BY and aggregates). v2.4.0 adds G016-G020 (FIRST and tie order independent of scan order, `score` as a SQL GROUP BY alias, HAVING precedence) and R014-R015 (V018). v2.3.0 adds `null_order_cases` (plain SELECT over the extra collections, ids in order) and runs `aggregate_cases` over the extra collections too, pinning where a NULL sort key lands. v2.2.0 adds the Euclidean `docs_l2` extra collection and the `e` query vector for vector GROUP BY cases, which may also pin each group's row (`expect_rows`), id (`expect_ids`) and score (`expect_scores`, within 1e-5).

cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs ORDER BY year ASC OFFSET 3

cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs ORDER BY year ASC LIMIT 2 OFFSET 10

cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR [0.8, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1] OR category = 'other' LIMIT 5
cases.note: NEAR under OR: the NEAR leaf is TRUE in a boolean context, so the disjunction admits every row and the NEAR ranking orders them (cosine to the query vector ranks all five rows apart). Core used to route this shape to the similarity() union executor, which dropped every NEAR hit and returned only the metadata side [3, 5], each scored 1.0

cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE (vector NEAR [0.8, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1] OR category = 'other') AND year >= 2021 LIMIT 5

known_bugs.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE year >= 2019 ORDER BY year DESC LIMIT 2
known_bugs.note: REGRESSION LOCK (fixed): scalar ORDER BY <column> + LIMIT previously applied the LIMIT before the sort on the bounded top-k path (returned [2,1] instead of [4,2]); the bounded path now equals the unbounded path truncated to k, per KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md #9. expect_ids is the correct, currently-asserted result.

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id WHERE customers.name = 'Alice' ORDER BY orders.id ASC

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM orders JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id ORDER BY orders.id ASC

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM orders_u JOIN customers_u USING (id) ORDER BY orders_u.id ASC
join_cases.note: issue #1544: JOIN USING (single column); both engines resolve USING(id) against each row's primary id, order_u id=99 has no matching customer and is dropped

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id ORDER BY orders.amount DESC
join_cases.note: ORDER BY sorts the JOINED rows, by a qualified column (core ordered the base rows first and could not read `orders.amount`; WASM ignored ORDER BY)

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id ORDER BY orders.id ASC LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1
join_cases.note: OFFSET and LIMIT window the joined rows

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM orders LEFT JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id WHERE customers.name = 'Alice' ORDER BY orders.id ASC
join_cases.note: a LEFT JOIN WHERE on the joined side reads the joined row (core filtered the base rows by it before the join and returned nothing)

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id WHERE customers.name = 'Bob' OR orders.amount = 100 ORDER BY orders.id ASC
join_cases.note: an OR across the base and a join side is evaluated on the joined row

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id WHERE NOT (customers.name = 'Alice') ORDER BY orders.id ASC
join_cases.note: a negated joined-side predicate is evaluated on the joined row

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM customers JOIN cities ON customers.name = cities.name ORDER BY customers.id ASC
join_cases.note: D014: an INNER JOIN on a non-primary-key column no index covers (core refused it for want of an index)

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM customers RIGHT JOIN cities ON customers.name = cities.name ORDER BY id ASC
join_cases.note: D014: RIGHT JOIN on any column; the city no customer matches (52) is a row of its own, with its own id (core required the primary key, WASM refused RIGHT JOIN)

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM customers FULL JOIN cities ON customers.name = cities.name ORDER BY id ASC
join_cases.note: D014: FULL JOIN keeps the unmatched customer (20) and the unmatched city (52)

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM customers_u RIGHT JOIN orders_u ON customers_u.id = orders_u.id ORDER BY id ASC
join_cases.note: a RIGHT JOIN on id = id keeps the unmatched joined row (99): core's id lookup shortcut answered it as an INNER join

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM customers RIGHT JOIN cities ON customers.name = cities.name WHERE customers.id IS NULL ORDER BY id ASC
join_cases.note: a RIGHT JOIN row without a base match reads the base side's id as NULL

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM left_rj RIGHT JOIN right_rj ON left_rj.k = right_rj.k LIMIT 1
join_cases.note: a RIGHT JOIN classifies a joined point as unmatched only against every base row: under LIMIT 1 core fetched base row 1 alone and returned point 7 as unmatched, though base row 2 matches it

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM left_rj RIGHT JOIN right_rj ON left_rj.k = right_rj.k WHERE left_rj.id = 99 ORDER BY id ASC
join_cases.note: a base-side WHERE filters the RIGHT JOIN's rows, not the base rows before it: core filtered the base first, so the matched point 7 came back as unmatched

join_cases.query: SELECT * FROM left_rj RIGHT JOIN right_rj ON left_rj.k = right_rj.k JOIN customers ON left_rj.id = customers.id ORDER BY id ASC
join_cases.note: a join after a RIGHT JOIN reads the base id as the row carries it: the unmatched point 10 has a NULL left_rj.id, and core's id lookup joined it to customer 10 by the row's own id

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY category ASC
aggregate_cases.note: issue #1544: GROUP BY with COUNT(*), executed via Database::execute_aggregate (core) / the default WASM SELECT pipeline. Uses an explicit AS alias; G010 covers the default names

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*) > 2 ORDER BY category ASC
aggregate_cases.note: issue #1544: GROUP BY + HAVING filters out groups that don't satisfy the aggregate predicate

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, SUM(year) AS total_year FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY category ASC
aggregate_cases.note: issue #1544: SUM aggregate per group

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(year) AS total_year FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY n DESC, category ASC
aggregate_cases.note: issue #1544: multiple aggregates per group and ORDER BY an aggregate column plus the group key. LIMIT on grouped rows is exercised by G005

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(year) AS total_year FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY n DESC, category ASC LIMIT 1
aggregate_cases.note: issue #1556: LIMIT applies to the ordered group rows in both engines (was documented_divergences D006 — core returned every group)

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY COUNT(*) ASC, category DESC LIMIT 1
aggregate_cases.note: ORDER BY repeats an aggregate the SELECT stores under an alias: both engines sort by the aliased column. Both used to look the row up under the aggregate's default name, compare every group as equal and fall through to the tie-breaker, which alone puts tech first

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, AVG(year) AS mean_year FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY AVG(year) ASC, category DESC
aggregate_cases.note: same as G006 for AVG

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs GROUP BY category HAVING SUM(year) > 5000 ORDER BY category ASC
aggregate_cases.note: HAVING tests an aggregate the SELECT does not list. Core used to accumulate only the SELECT's aggregates, read SUM(year) as absent and drop every group; WASM computed it

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS year FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY year DESC
aggregate_cases.note: ORDER BY `year` names the count, the aggregate aliased `year`; the payload field `year` is not a column of the grouped rows

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, COUNT(*), SUM(year), AVG(year) FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY count DESC
aggregate_cases.note: unaliased aggregates carry the same default names in both engines (AggregateFunction::result_key), and ORDER BY can name them. WASM used to output count(*), sum(year) and avg(year) (formerly documented_divergences D001)

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, COUNT(category) AS n FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY category ASC
aggregate_cases.note: COUNT(column) counts the non-null values of any type; core counted numeric values only and returned 0 for a string column

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, year, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY category ASC
aggregate_cases.note: a grouped row carries its GROUP BY columns and aggregates only; WASM used to add a selected column outside GROUP BY from the group's first row

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs GROUP BY id ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 2
aggregate_cases.note: a GROUP BY column resolves as in WHERE: `id` is the point id (core read a payload field `id` and put every row in one NULL group)

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT grp, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs_l2 GROUP BY grp ORDER BY grp ASC
aggregate_cases.note: ORDER BY puts NULL last in ASC (core sorted it first)

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT grp, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs_l2 GROUP BY grp ORDER BY grp DESC
aggregate_cases.note: and first in DESC (core sorted it last)

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, FIRST(year) AS y FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY category ASC
aggregate_cases.note: outside a vector GROUP BY, FIRST reads the group's row with the smallest point id (other: id 3, tech: id 1), whatever order the engine scans in

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, AVG(year) AS score FROM docs GROUP BY category ORDER BY category ASC
aggregate_cases.note: a SQL GROUP BY may name an aggregate `score` or `id`; only a vector GROUP BY, whose groups carry their own, refuses it (V017)

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT grp, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs_l2 GROUP BY grp ORDER BY n DESC
aggregate_cases.note: groups equal on every ORDER BY key fall back to their GROUP BY key, ascending (y before NULL)

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT year, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs GROUP BY year
aggregate_cases.note: without ORDER BY, SQL GROUP BY groups come by GROUP BY key ascending (core returned hash order, WASM scan order)

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM docs GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*) = 2 OR COUNT(*) > 0 AND COUNT(*) > 5
aggregate_cases.note: HAVING AND binds tighter than OR, as in SQL: n = 2 OR (n > 0 AND n > 5). Read left to right, the condition kept no group

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT kind, COUNT(id) AS n, MAX(id) AS top FROM tickets WHERE id >= 32 GROUP BY kind
aggregate_cases.note: the WHERE of an aggregate reads `id` as the point id, as its aggregates do, although every payload carries an `id` of its own

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT x, COUNT(*) AS n FROM nums WHERE id <= 4 GROUP BY x
aggregate_cases.note: `-0.0` and `0` are one group, `1.0` and `1` another, each keyed by its integer

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT x, MIN(x) AS low, MAX(x) AS top FROM nums WHERE id <= 4 GROUP BY x
aggregate_cases.note: MIN and MAX of values equal by value return the integer, whichever row comes first (`-0.0` and `1.0` come first here)

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT x, MAX(x) AS top FROM nums GROUP BY x HAVING MAX(x) > 9007199254740992.0
aggregate_cases.note: HAVING compares an integer aggregate with a float threshold exactly, as WHERE does: 2^53 + 1 is greater than the float 2^53

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT x, COUNT(*) AS n FROM nums GROUP BY x HAVING MAX(x) = 0.3
SELECT customers.name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id GROUP BY customers.name ORDER BY customers.name ASC
aggregate_cases.note: a GROUP BY over a JOIN groups the joined rows, by a qualified column (core aggregated the base collection alone: one group, n = 4, name null)

aggregate_cases.query: SELECT orders.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(orders.amount) AS total FROM orders LEFT JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id WHERE customers.id IS NULL GROUP BY orders.customer_id
aggregate_cases.note: a LEFT JOIN row without a match carries its alias with a null id, so WHERE customers.id IS NULL finds order 4, whose customer 99 does not exist

setops_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'tech' ORDER BY year ASC UNION SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'other' ORDER BY year ASC
setops_cases.note: UNION of two disjoint partitions returns every id once; the last operand's ORDER BY windows the compound, so the rows come back by year (velesql::execute_compound)

setops_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'tech' ORDER BY year ASC UNION SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'tech' ORDER BY year ASC
setops_cases.note: UNION of a branch with itself proves de-duplication (3 rows, not 6)

setops_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE year >= 2020 ORDER BY year ASC INTERSECT SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'tech' ORDER BY year ASC
setops_cases.note: INTERSECT keeps the rows present in both branches, ordered by the window

setops_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs ORDER BY year ASC EXCEPT SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'other' ORDER BY year ASC
setops_cases.note: EXCEPT removes the right-hand branch's rows from the left-hand branch

setops_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'tech' UNION SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'other' LIMIT 2
setops_cases.note: a LIMIT after the last operand windows the compound (core ignored it: the trailing LIMIT was the last operand's, overridden). Without ORDER BY the metadata rows tie at 1.0 and keep the order met

setops_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'tech' ORDER BY year DESC LIMIT 1 UNION SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'other' ORDER BY year ASC
setops_cases.note: a first operand keeps its own ORDER BY / LIMIT (tech's latest year, 4); the last operand's ORDER BY windows the compound

setops_cases.query: SELECT category FROM docs WHERE year >= 2021 INTERSECT SELECT category FROM docs WHERE year <= 2020
setops_cases.note: rows are compared by their projected values: both year ranges hold a tech and an other category, so both survive the INTERSECT (as the first rows met with them, 2 and 3)

setops_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs_l2 WHERE vector NEAR $e LIMIT 2 UNION SELECT * FROM docs_l2 WHERE grp = 'y'
setops_cases.note: without ORDER BY the rows rank by score in the metric's direction — closest first under euclidean (24 at 0.5, then the ties at 1.0 in the order met)

match_cases.query: MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person) RETURN a ORDER BY a.id ASC
match_cases.note: issue #1544: 1-hop MATCH, one query text for both engines: the target collection comes from `_collection`, and each row's `a` binding is compared. Both engines hold the SAME topology (chain 1->2->3->4, label KNOWS); only where the edges are stored differs (D004)

match_cases.query: MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(c:Person) RETURN a ORDER BY a.id ASC
match_cases.note: issue #1544: 2-hop MATCH over the same chain topology as M001

match_cases.query: MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(:Person) RETURN a ORDER BY a.id ASC
match_cases.note: an unnamed node binds no name: one row per distinct binding of the named nodes
inline pattern properties filter as WHERE `=` does, a `$name` taking the caller's value
a bare WHERE column reads the walk's target, the last node

match_cases.query: MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person) RETURN a ORDER BY id * -1
match_cases.note: an arithmetic MATCH ORDER BY reads the row's target (b = 4, 3, 2 here), through core's ScoreContext in both engines (WASM refused arithmetic)

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR $a LIMIT 5
near_cases.note: NEAR ranks every point by cosine similarity to $a; $a was chosen so no two points tie

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR $a LIMIT 2
near_cases.note: NEAR + LIMIT keeps the k best

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR $a LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1
near_cases.note: OFFSET on a ranked result skips the best hit

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR $a AND category = 'tech' LIMIT 5
near_cases.note: hybrid NEAR + metadata: the predicate is a hard filter and the vector ranking is kept

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR $a AND (category = 'other' OR year = 2020) LIMIT 5
near_cases.note: hybrid NEAR + a parenthesized OR filter

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR $a ORDER BY similarity() ASC LIMIT 5
near_cases.note: ORDER BY similarity() ASC reverses the natural ranking

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR $a ORDER BY year ASC LIMIT 5
near_cases.note: ORDER BY a payload column re-orders the NEAR hits and keeps each hit's similarity score

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR $a AND similarity(vector, $a) > 0.5 LIMIT 5
near_cases.note: NEAR + similarity() threshold on the same vector

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE similarity(vector, $a) > 0.35 LIMIT 5
near_cases.note: similarity() threshold without NEAR: rows are ranked by that similarity and carry it as their score (was documented_divergences D011)

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE similarity(vector, $a) > 0.35 ORDER BY year ASC
near_cases.note: similarity() threshold + ORDER BY a column: the column decides the order, the score is still the similarity

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE similarity(vector, $a) > 0.35 AND category = 'tech' ORDER BY year ASC
near_cases.note: similarity() threshold combined with a metadata predicate

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE similarity(vector, $a) <= 0.35 ORDER BY year ASC
near_cases.note: similarity() upper bound

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs_l2 WHERE similarity(vector, $e) > 1.5 ORDER BY id ASC
near_cases.note: under a distance metric `similarity() > t` keeps the rows CLOSER than t: docs_l2 sits at distances 1, 3, 2, 0.5 from $e

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs_l2 WHERE similarity(vector, $e) <= 1.5 ORDER BY id ASC
near_cases.note: the complement of N013: not closer than 1.5

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs_l2 WHERE similarity(vector, $e) = 2.0
near_cases.note: equality allows velesql::SIMILARITY_EQ_TOLERANCE

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM named WHERE similarity(alt, $x) > 0.5 ORDER BY id ASC
near_cases.note: a named vector: similarity(alt, $x) scores the payload's `alt` array; a row without one (44) or with another dimension (45) cannot be scored, so the leaf is UNKNOWN there

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM named WHERE NOT similarity(alt, $x) > 0.5 ORDER BY id ASC
near_cases.note: NOT of an UNKNOWN leaf is UNKNOWN: 44 and 45 stay out of the complement too

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM named WHERE similarity(vector, $x) > 0.5 AND similarity(alt, $y) > 0.5 ORDER BY id ASC
near_cases.note: two similarity() leaves on different vectors filter in cascade: 43 passes the first (0.707) but not the second (0.447)

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM named WHERE similarity(vector, $x) > 0.5 AND similarity(vector, $y) > 0.5
near_cases.note: two query vectors on the row's own vector: each leaf is scored against its own vector (WASM used to refuse distinct vectors)

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM named WHERE similarity(vector, $x) > 0.5 AND similarity(alt, $x) > 0.5
near_cases.note: a row carries its FIRST similarity() leaf's score: 43 is 0.707 from $x by its own vector, 0.894 by `alt` (core used to report the last leaf's)

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM named WHERE similarity(alt, $x) > 0.5 AND similarity(vector, $x) > 0.5
near_cases.note: N020 with the leaves swapped: the score follows the first leaf

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR $a AND similarity(vector, $b) > 0.3 LIMIT 5
near_cases.note: NEAR ranks the rows and gives their score; the similarity() threshold only filters (ids 3 and 4 are within 0.3 of $b). Core used to report each row's similarity to $b while ranking by NEAR

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE category = 'other' ORDER BY year ASC
near_cases.note: a row no vector predicate scored carries velesql::METADATA_MATCH_SCORE on both engines (D009; WASM reported 0.0)

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs_l2 WHERE similarity(vector, $e) > 0.8 OR grp = 'y'
near_cases.note: a threshold OR-ed with metadata: every row is scored by its real distance and ranked closest first (24 passes the threshold, 22 the predicate). Core scored the metadata side 1.0 and sorted descending whatever the metric

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE NOT similarity(vector, $a) > 0.5 LIMIT 3
near_cases.note: a negated threshold ranks by the similarity, best first, and LIMIT keeps the best (core returned the lowest ids)

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM named WHERE similarity(alt, $x) > 0.5
near_cases.note: without NEAR the rows are ranked by the named vector the threshold reads (core ranked a window of points near $x by their own vectors)

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM named WHERE similarity(alt, $x) > 0.5 OR id = 44
near_cases.note: a row the first similarity() cannot score (44 has no `alt`) passes through the OR, ranks after the scored rows and carries velesql::METADATA_MATCH_SCORE

near_cases.query: SELECT * FROM docs WHERE vector NEAR $a ORDER BY vector_score ASC LIMIT 3
near_cases.note: `vector_score` is the NEAR row's vector component in both engines (WASM read it as a payload field)

documented_divergences.area: MATCH edge storage (core unified vs WASM separate graph store)
documented_divergences.core_behavior: graph nodes ARE collection points (payload `_labels` field); edges live on the same Collection via add_edge
documented_divergences.wasm_behavior: edges live in a separate in-memory graph store per name (`INSERT EDGE`, `WasmDatabase.addEdge`); the nodes a MATCH binds are, as in core, the points of the collection with that name, plus nodes written with `INSERT NODE`, which win on a shared id. Everything a query can observe is the same: the target comes from `_collection`, `@collection` adds properties, and the same MATCH text returns the same rows
documented_divergences.status: accepted architectural difference, storage only: fixture match_cases run ONE query text on both engines; each harness only loads the shared topology its own way

It used to run in the aggregation pipeline, which ignored ORDER BY, had no default LIMIT, and keyed `DISTINCT *` on id and score so no row ever collapsed
documented_divergences.status: resolved — projection_cases P001-P004 assert the projected rows on both engines

documented_divergences.core_behavior: `USING FUSION (strategy='weighted'|'weighted_rrf'|'rsf')` executes over real scored branches (BM25 text MATCH, SPARSE_NEAR, graph) once core's QueryValidator counts two fusable branches
documented_divergences.wasm_behavior: NEAR + SPARSE_NEAR runs core's dense + sparse fusion (velesql_sparse.rs), every strategy included, with core's strategy mapping (FusionClause::dense_sparse_strategy) and branch directions; velesql_sparse_parity_tests.rs pins ids and scores against a core Database. Beside a NEAR without a SPARSE_NEAR, a weight-sensitive strategy is refused outright by reject_single_branch_weighted_fusion (velesql_select.rs): WASM's only second branch there is a synthetic constant-1.0 id-equality hit set, so a weight-sensitive fusion would rank noise; 'rrf'/'average'/'maximum' still execute over that synthetic branch as a hard-filtered no-op (demo parity). No core-answer/wasm-refuse pair is reachable in practice: the one other branch type that would make the strategies meaningful (MATCH BM25) is unsupported in WASM WHERE evaluation and fails earlier. `multi_query_search` (the JS API, store_search.rs) DOES accept weighted_rrf via its `weights` argument — this refusal is VelesQL-surface only
documented_divergences.status: accepted — the refusal is the designed guard, not a missing feature (#2095 A3 residual audit, 2026-11-07)
documented_divergences.evidence: crates/velesdb-wasm/src/velesql_sparse.rs (NEAR + SPARSE_NEAR fusion); crates/velesdb-wasm/src/velesql_select.rs: reject_single_branch_weighted_fusion(); crates/velesdb-wasm/src/velesql_fusion.rs (synthetic payload branch); crates/velesdb-wasm/src/velesql_where.rs (MATCH BM25 unsupported); crates/velesdb-wasm/src/store_search.rs (weighted_rrf accepted on multi_query_search)
